commitResults.messageTitle: Rename Duke to Suki and add greeting
Add support for echo
Add support for storing and listing tasks
Add support for marking and unmarking tasks
Add Task class to represent tasks
Add support for todo, deadline and event tasks
Add error handling with SukiException
Add support for deleting tasks and switch to ArrayList
Use CommandType enum for command dispatch
Add saving and loading of tasks to disk
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks were held only in memory, so the list was lost whenever the
program exited. Add a Storage class that owns reading and writing a
plain-text save file at data/suki.txt, keeping file I/O out of Suki
itself.

Tasks are loaded once at startup and the whole list is rewritten after
every command that succeeds. Rewriting the file is wasteful compared to
appending, but the list is small and this keeps the file correct after
deletes and marks without any extra bookkeeping.

A missing save file is treated as an empty list, and unparseable lines
are skipped, so a damaged file costs at most the bad entries rather than
preventing startup.

commitResults.messageTitle: Understand dates and times instead of storing them as text
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and Event kept whatever text the user typed, so "Sunday" and
"2019-10-15" were equally opaque: they could be shown back but never
compared, sorted or reformatted.

Introduce a DateTime value class that parses the common written forms
(yyyy-MM-dd and d/M/yyyy, each optionally with a 24-hour time) and
prints them in the friendlier "Oct 15 2019, 6:00PM" style.

DateTime wraps LocalDateTime rather than exposing it directly so it can
remember whether the user supplied a time. Storing a bare LocalDateTime
would have been less code, but every date-only deadline would then print
a misleading "12:00AM". It implements Comparable so later increments can
sort or filter by date without touching this class again.

Unparseable input now produces a message naming the accepted formats
rather than being silently accepted as a label.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
commitResults.messageBody:
Git merged the two branches without reporting a conflict, but the result
did not compile: Level-7 added getters returning String while Level-8
changed the same fields to DateTime, and the two edits were far enough
apart in the file that the textual merge saw no overlap.

Resolve by keeping Level-8's types and widening the Level-7 getters to
match. Storage now writes dates via DateTime#toStorageString and reads
them back via DateTime#parse, so a saved time of day survives a reload
instead of being flattened to text.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split Suki into Ui, Parser and TaskList collaborators
commitResults.messageBody:
Suki had grown into a single class that read input, printed output,
picked apart command syntax, held the task list and enforced its bounds.
Every new feature meant editing the same long switch, and none of that
logic could be exercised without driving the console.

Give each responsibility its own class:

- Ui owns all reading and printing, so console formatting is replaceable
  in one place and the rest of the program never calls System.out.
- Parser owns the command syntax, so knowledge of where the slashes go
  stops leaking into the main loop.
- TaskList owns the tasks and their index checking, which previously had
  to be repeated by each caller.

Suki keeps only the wiring and the main loop, and becomes an instance
rather than a pile of statics so its collaborators can be fields.

A fuller alternative is the Command pattern, where Parser returns a
Command object that executes itself and the switch disappears entirely.
That is the better design once commands grow their own state, but it
adds a class per command for no gain at the current size, so the switch
stays for now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move all classes into a suki package
commitResults.messageBody:
The twelve classes sat in the default package, which Java allows but
which offers no namespace: any class added later, by this project or by
a library on the classpath, competes for the same bare names.

Put them in a package named suki. This costs one line per file and
changes the entry point to suki.Suki, but it groups the project's
classes under a name of their own and is a precondition for the jar
built in a later increment being safely combinable with other code.

The package is deliberately flat rather than split into sub-packages
such as suki.task and suki.parser. At twelve classes the extra structure
would add import noise without making anything easier to find; splitting
becomes worthwhile when the class count grows.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for the parsing, list and storage classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Every change so far was checked by typing commands at the program and
reading the output, which is slow and only ever exercises the paths
someone remembers to try.

Add 36 JUnit 5 tests over the classes where the logic actually lives:

- DateTimeTest covers each accepted input format, the round trip through
  toStorageString, and chronological ordering.
- ParserTest covers well-formed commands and the malformed ones that
  should produce a readable error.
- TaskListTest covers the centralised bounds checking.
- TaskTest pins the display text the list command depends on.
- StorageTest saves and reloads through a JUnit @TempDir, so the tests
  never touch the real data/suki.txt.

Writing these immediately found a bug: DateTime accepted 2019-02-31 and
silently turned it into 28 February, because patterns built with
ofPattern resolve in SMART mode and clamp out-of-range days. The
formatters now resolve strictly, which required changing the year field
from yyyy to uuuu, and such dates are rejected.

The project has no build tool yet, so the JUnit console jar is fetched
into lib/ and gitignored rather than committed; A-Gradle will replace
this with a declared dependency. Commands to compile and run the suite
are in the README.

commitResults.messageTitle: Package the application as a runnable JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
Running Suki previously meant compiling the sources and knowing the
right classpath and entry point, which makes it awkward to hand to
anyone who is not working on the code.

Build a JAR whose manifest names suki.Suki as the Main-Class, so it runs
with a bare "java -jar". The JAR is produced with the jar tool rather
than an IDE artifact configuration so that the exact command is written
down and reproducible; it goes to build/, which is gitignored, because a
build product should not be tracked alongside its sources.

Verified by running it from an unrelated working directory: it starts,
accepts commands, and creates data/suki.txt relative to wherever it was
launched.

Also document the compile, test and jar commands in the README, and fix
the stale path to Suki.java left over from the move into the suki
package.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document all classes, methods and fields with Javadoc
commitResults.messageBody:
Roughly half the code carried no Javadoc: the classes written early had
only a one-line class comment, and the accessors and Ui methods added
later had none at all. Anyone reading Task or Ui had to infer from the
body what a method promised.

Add Javadoc across all twelve classes, covering every class, method and
field including the private ones, with @param, @return and @throws where
they apply. Points worth stating rather than restating are called out:
that getTypeIcon doubles as the save-file type field, that asArrayList
returns the live list rather than a copy, and that SukiException carries
text meant for the user rather than a developer.

Verified with "javadoc -Xdoclint:all -private", which reports no
warnings; that flag is what caught the last few missing @return tags and
undocumented constants.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the coding standard: declaration order and named constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Checked the code against the module's checkstyle ruleset rather than by
eye, which turned up two kinds of problem.

DateTime declared its instance fields and constructor in the middle of
the class, after a static helper. The standard order is static fields,
instance fields, constructors, then methods, so the helper moves below
the constructor.

Parser and Storage repeated bare literals: " /by ", " /from " and " /to "
appeared inline in the split calls, and the save-file type codes "T",
"D", "E" and the done flags "1" and "0" were written out at both the
encoding and decoding sites. Each is now a named constant, so the two
sides of the file format cannot drift apart silently and the delimiters
are stated once.

Parser also gains a private constructor, since it holds only static
helpers and was never meant to be instantiated.

The only violations the ruleset still reports are missing Javadoc, which
is the subject of a separate branch.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command for searching tasks by description
commitResults.messageBody:
Once the list grows past a screenful, the only way to locate a task is
to read the whole thing, which also makes it hard to pick the right
number for mark or delete.

Add "find <keyword>", which shows the tasks whose description contains
the keyword. Matching is case-insensitive and works on substrings, so
"find book" finds both "read book" and "Return Book to library".

Only the description is searched. Including the formatted dates was
considered and rejected: a user searching for "oct" would get every task
due in October, which is surprising when they meant the word.

TaskList#find returns a new TaskList rather than filtering in place, so
searching never disturbs the real list, and the numbers shown are
positions within the results.

Covered by eight tests in FindTest, including that the original list is
left untouched and that dates are excluded from matching.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
commitResults.messageBody:
Both branches edited the same region of DateTime: one added Javadoc to
the strict() helper and the instance fields, the other moved strict()
below the constructor to satisfy the declaration-order rule.

Resolve by taking both — the coding-standard ordering, with the Javadoc
carried onto strict() in its new position. Checkstyle now reports no
violations, since the missing-Javadoc errors left by the previous branch
are supplied by this one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
commitResults.messageBody:
Three files conflicted, all because this branch added a member exactly
where the earlier branches had added Javadoc:

- CommandType: the constants list was rewritten one-per-line with a
  comment each, while this branch added FIND to the single-line form.
  Resolved by keeping the documented form and giving FIND a comment too.
- Parser and Ui: parseFindKeyword and showFoundTasks were each inserted
  immediately before a method whose Javadoc had just been written, so
  git saw one comment block being replaced by another. Resolved by
  keeping both members with their own documentation.

None of these were competing changes; they only looked like it because
they touched adjacent lines. Verified after resolving: 44 tests pass,
checkstyle reports no violations, and javadoc runs clean under
-Xdoclint:all.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs for the console messages
commitResults.messageBody:
Suki's replies are fixed sequences of lines whose length varies from one
message to the next: an error is one line, a task confirmation three,
the greeting five. Each Ui method spelled this out as its own run of
System.out.println calls, which repeated the same printing in nine
places and tied nine methods to System.out individually.

Replace those with a single show(String... lines). Varargs fits better
than an array or list parameter here because every caller passes lines
known at the call site, so each message becomes one call that lists its
lines, with nothing having to build a collection first.

showTaskCount becomes taskCountMessage, returning its line rather than
printing it, so that the add and remove confirmations remain a single
call to show rather than a print followed by a helper call.

Behaviour is unchanged: a 13-command session covering every command and
both error paths produces byte-identical output before and after, and
all 44 tests still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Varargs'
Add Gradle support
commitResults.messageBody:
The project had no build tool: compiling, testing and packaging were all
done by hand with javac and jar, and the JUnit console launcher had to be
downloaded separately before the tests could run at all. That is fragile
and does not carry over to another machine.

Bring in the Gradle wrapper by merging the course's add-gradle-support
branch, as the Gradle tutorial directs, rather than writing a build file
from scratch. Merging keeps the wrapper, its properties and the supplied
build.gradle exactly as issued, so the build behaves the same here as it
does for everyone else on the module.

Two project-specific edits on top of the supplied file:

- application.mainClass points at suki.Suki instead of the placeholder
  seedu.duke.Duke.
- shadowJar produces suki.jar rather than duke.jar.

Committing the wrapper is deliberate: it is what lets someone clone the
repository and build it without installing Gradle first.

The README's build section is rewritten accordingly, dropping the manual
javac invocations and the JUnit download step.

Verified: all 44 tests pass under "gradlew test", and the jar produced by
"gradlew shadowJar" gives byte-identical output to the previous hand-built
one over the same 13-command session.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Gradle'
Add a JavaFX GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
Suki could only be used from a console. This adds the GUI from the
JavaFX tutorial: a scrolling conversation of dialog boxes, each showing
an avatar beside what was said, with a text field and Send button.

Structure follows part 4 of the tutorial rather than part 2, so the
layout lives in FXML (MainWindow.fxml, DialogBox.fxml) instead of being
built by hand in Java. That keeps look separate from behaviour and means
the window can be adjusted in Scene Builder without touching code.

Launcher exists only because the JavaFX runtime refuses to start when the
class holding main is itself an Application and JavaFX is on the
classpath rather than the module path. application.mainClass therefore
points at suki.Launcher.

The dependency block and the launcher/FXML arrangement are taken from the
tutorial as written, deliberately: mixing approaches here tends to
produce a build that works on one machine and fails on other operating
systems.

Connecting the GUI needed a way to get a reply back as a string rather
than printed. Because the previous increment funnelled every line through
Ui.show, that was small: Ui now also records what it shows, and
takeOutput returns and clears the record. Suki.getResponse runs one line
through the same execute method the console loop uses, so the two front
ends cannot drift apart in behaviour.

showWelcome and showGoodbye are split so the GUI can show the greeting
and farewell without the ASCII banner and horizontal rules, which only
make sense in a console.

The text interface is kept, as the module suggests, because the core
logic is far easier to test through it than through a window.

Verified: gradlew build passes with all 44 tests, the console front end
produces byte-identical output to before over the same 13-command
session, and every fx:id, handler and resource path referenced by the
FXML resolves against the controllers and the packaged jar.
